document.title: Afghanistan: Taliban Seem to Have Less Funds and Supplies This Year, But the Problem Does Not Appear to be that Acute (Islama 01320)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
document.note: [Confidential] Under post-nuclear-test sanctions Pakistan reduced Taliban aid, though it still wrote a check of about a million dollars every couple of months. Saudi private donations fell, bin Laden gave the Taliban some money, and Masoud remains well funded by Iran, Russia, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.

events.description: Pakistan's nuclear tests led to sanctions and economic problems that reduced aid to the Taliban.
Taliban captured NIMA supply depots at Maimana.
Taliban captured NIMA depots at Shiberghan and took Mazar-i-Sharif, aided by bribes.
Taliban seized an Ismaili militia depot in the Kayan Valley and took Bamiyan.
Saudi government blocked private Saudi funding to the Taliban after a rift over Bin Ladin.
A source told the Embassy that Taliban logistics commanders were short of ammunition and spare parts.
Pakistan conducted nuclear tests; sanctions worsened its economy, reducing aid to Taliban.
Taliban captured supply depots in Maimana (Faryab) when entering the area.
Taliban captured supply depots at Shiberghan (Jozjan) and took Mazar-i-Sharif.
Taliban seized large depot from Ismaili militia in Kayan Valley and captured Bamiyan.
Saudi government implemented measures cutting private funding to the Taliban amid open rift over bin Ladin.
A source told the Embassy political officer that Taliban logistics commanders were running low on ammunition and spare parts.
Taliban expected to launch large-scale warm-weather offensive against Massoud/Jamiat from late April.
Pakistan's nuclear tests led to sanctions causing grave economic problems that reduced funds for the Taliban.
Taliban military offensive late 1998 seized much territory, overstretching logistics.
Source told the US Embassy POLOFF that Taliban logisticians were running low on ammunition and spare parts.
US Embassy Islamabad sends cable Islama 01320 on Taliban funding and supply problems.

key_claims: The Taliban have less money and supplies in early 1999 because Pakistan and Middle Eastern donors have reduced support.
Pakistan's reduced aid is attributed to its own economic problems after the May 1998 nuclear test sanctions, not to deliberate pressure on the Taliban.
Saudi Arabia cut private funding in September 1998 over Kandahar's harboring of Bin Ladin.
The Taliban still receive funds from private UAE and Qatari sources, narcotics traffickers and customs revenue.
Taliban supplies are bought on the UAE grey arms market, and Taliban captured depots in the 1998 offensive eased shortages.
Jamiat under Massoud is well funded by Iran, which delivers via Tajikistan, and uses the cash to bribe Taliban commanders.
Massoud's dependence on outside patrons makes him more vulnerable than the Taliban to their whims.
